text: The story of the value discrepancy at the core
of CENTS is told in the traits of Cent #1264.
The starting point for Rutherford Chang,
the fact that the copper in one penny
was worth about 3 times as much as a penny,
has roots and implications that are
activated by the system that he created with CENTS.
In July 1944, at Bretton Woods,
44 nations tied their currencies to the US
dollar, and the dollar to gold,
at 35 dollars an ounce.
Gold was the measure of money.
On August 15, 1971, the United States
stopped exchanging dollars for gold.
"Your dollar will be worth just
as much tomorrow as it is today."
Within two years the Bretton Woods system
had collapsed, and currencies
floated against each other.
US currency became fiat:
worth what it is trusted to be worth.
Dislocating the global reserve
currency from any material substance
had wide-ranging effects,
not only on wealth distribution
and social equity,
but on materiality itself.
These effects continue to bear
influence to this day, in economics
as well as art.
In the words of Adina Glickstein,
in her article "Never Midcurve" for Spike
Magazine: "Post-Bretton
Woods as much as post-internet,
hasn't contemporary art become,
if not exactly a commercial product,
the financial instrument par excellence?"
It is in the strange tension between 20th
century conceptual art and 21st
century post-internet art,
between absence of an object
and digital objecthood,
between value discrepancy and speculation,
that CENTS resides.
Among collectors, coins from years
that are significant to the project's
concept have acquired a special resonance.
22 of the 10,000 Cents are dated 1944.
None is dated 1943,
the year pennies were struck in steel.
1944 also makes this a Wheat Cent,
one of 208: from 1909 to 1958,
two ears of wheat framed the back of the penny.
This Cent is the oldest Gold
Cent in the collection, by 12 years.
The Traits Atlas of the CENTS Trait Council
describes gold patina as a luminous surface
toning, suspended between metal and light.
This one is Notable Gold.
69 Cents carry gold.
Every other one was struck in 1956 or later.
Over Lincoln's head lies Significant Obsidian:
in the Atlas's words, a major visual actor
with strong darkening, but not yet fully dominant.
The unique form of the obsidian on this
Cent is what gives it its nickname: the Alien Cent.
Near the rim, a fleck of paint
marks it as Contaminated.
Compare Cent #543,
also from 1944, with no visual trait.
Two very different histories within one history.
Struck in the year the dollar was tied to gold,
and bearing the marks of all that's come between.
Cent #1264, a great Cent.
